claim: The spatial distribution of atrophy in neurodegenerative diseases suggests that brain connectivity mediates disease propagation.
source: The spatial distribution of atrophy in neurodegenerative diseases suggests that brain connectivity mediates disease propagation.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior work.

claim: Topological profiles explain the observed data better than single descriptors.
source: Experimental results comparing topological profiles for Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis and normal ageing show that topological profiles explain the observed data better than single descriptors.
evidence: Supported by AIC scores and variance explained percentages presented in the Results section and Figure 2.

claim: Within each condition, most individual profiles cluster around the cohort-level profile.
source: Within each condition, most individual profiles cluster around the cohort-level profile, and individuals whose profiles align more closely with other cohort-level profiles show features of that cohort.
evidence: Demonstrated by the ternary plots and tSNE visualizations in Figure 3 and classification rates in Table 3.

claim: Individuals whose profiles align more closely with other cohort-level profiles show features of that cohort.
source: Within each condition, most individual profiles cluster around the cohort-level profile, and individuals whose profiles align more closely with other cohort-level profiles show features of that cohort.
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analyses showing AD outliers closer to HA have higher MMSE scores and HA outliers closer to AD have lower MMSE scores.

claim: Atrophy patterns observed with MRI suggest that different brain regions are systematically and selectively vulnerable to different neurodegenerative diseases.
source: For example, atrophy patterns observed with MRI suggest that different brain regions are systematically and selectively vulnerable to different neurodegenerative diseases, and that these atrophy patterns closely match known connectivity networks (Iturria-Medina, 2013; Iturria-Medina and Evans, 2015; Raj et al., 2012; Seeley et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Atrophy patterns closely match known connectivity networks.
source: For example, atrophy patterns observed with MRI suggest that different brain regions are systematically and selectively vulnerable to different neurodegenerative diseases, and that these atrophy patterns closely match known connectivity networks (Iturria-Medina, 2013; Iturria-Medina and Evans, 2015; Raj et al., 2012; Seeley et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In Alzheimer's disease, Zhou et al. (2012) attempt to explain the association between patterns of brain atrophy and connectivity in terms of different topological descriptors: centrality, segregation, network proximity, and cortical proximity.
source: Indeed, in Alzheimer's disease (AD), Zhou et al. (2012) attempt to explain the association between patterns of brain atrophy and connectivity in terms of different topological descriptors: (1) centrality – the most active regions or 'hubs' are most vulnerable (Buckner et al., 2009; Saxena and Caroni, 2011); (2) segregation – opposite to 1), the most isolated nodes are most vulnerable (Appel, 1981; Salehi et al., 2006); (3) network proximity – regions connected to disease epicenters are most vulnerable (Frost and Diamond, 2010; Jucker and Walker, 2013; Prusiner, 1984); (4) cortical proximity – regions spatially adjacent to disease epicenters are most vulnerable.
evidence: Direct citation to Zhou et al. (2012) and supporting references for each descriptor.

claim: Centrality represents nodal stress as a mechanism of pathology propagation.
source: The authors relate these descriptors to distinct mechanisms of pathology propagation: (1) centrality represents nodal stress, (2) segregation, trophic failure, (3) network proximity, trans-neuronal spread, and (4) cortical proximity represents unguided diffusive propagation.
evidence: Based on interpretation from Zhou et al. (2012) as cited in the text.

claim: Segregation represents trophic failure as a mechanism of pathology propagation.
source: The authors relate these descriptors to distinct mechanisms of pathology propagation: (1) centrality represents nodal stress, (2) segregation, trophic failure, (3) network proximity, trans-neuronal spread, and (4) cortical proximity represents unguided diffusive propagation.
evidence: Based on interpretation from Zhou et al. (2012) as cited in the text.

claim: Network proximity represents trans-neuronal spread as a mechanism of pathology propagation.
source: The authors relate these descriptors to distinct mechanisms of pathology propagation: (1) centrality represents nodal stress, (2) segregation, trophic failure, (3) network proximity, trans-neuronal spread, and (4) cortical proximity represents unguided diffusive propagation.
evidence: Based on interpretation from Zhou et al. (2012) as cited in the text.

claim: Cortical proximity represents unguided diffusive propagation as a mechanism of pathology propagation.
source: The authors relate these descriptors to distinct mechanisms of pathology propagation: (1) centrality represents nodal stress, (2) segregation, trophic failure, (3) network proximity, trans-neuronal spread, and (4) cortical proximity represents unguided diffusive propagation.
evidence: Based on interpretation from Zhou et al. (2012) as cited in the text.

claim: Previous studies have focused on evaluating the ability of each individual topological descriptor to explain observed patient data with the goal of identifying the single most likely mechanism of disease propagation.
source: Previous studies (Iturria-Medina, 2013; Iturria-Medina and Evans, 2015; Seeley et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2012; Saxena and Caroni, 2011; Buckner, 2005; Cope et al., 2018; Fornito et al., 2015; Mancini, 2016) using functional or structural networks have focused on evaluating the ability of each individual topological descriptor above to explain observed patient data with the goal of identifying the single most likely mechanism of disease propagation.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Previous approaches do not consider the possibility of multiple concurrent spreading mechanisms.
source: Two key limitations are: i) the approaches do not consider the possibility of multiple concurrent spreading mechanisms; ii) the evaluation of topological descriptors is performed using only cross-sectional data assumed to represent end-stage atrophy patterns.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior work based on the authors' review of the literature.

claim: The evaluation of topological descriptors in previous approaches is performed using only cross-sectional data assumed to represent end-stage atrophy patterns.
source: Two key limitations are: i) the approaches do not consider the possibility of multiple concurrent spreading mechanisms; ii) the evaluation of topological descriptors is performed using only cross-sectional data assumed to represent end-stage atrophy patterns.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior work based on the authors' review of the literature.

claim: Multiple distinct mechanisms are likely to contribute in diseases where multiple proteinopathies are at play, such as amyloid and tau in AD.
source: Regarding limitation (i), multiple distinct mechanisms are likely to contribute in diseases where multiple proteinopathies are at play (such as amyloid and tau in AD; see for example Iaccarino et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2016; Leal et al., 2018);
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on multiple proteinopathies in AD.

claim: Multiple sclerosis exhibits highly-variable atrophy patterns.
source: in diseases exhibiting highly-variable atrophy patterns (as in multiple sclerosis (MS); see Steenwijk et al., 2016);
evidence: Supported by citation to Steenwijk et al., 2016.

claim: Tau accumulation occurs in Parkinson's disease.
source: or in individual cases where multiple pathologies co-exist, as for instance tau accumulation in Parkinson's disease (Irwin et al., 2013; Lei et al., 2010),
evidence: Supported by citations to Irwin et al., 2013 and Lei et al., 2010.

claim: Alpha-synuclein or TDP-43 can occur in AD.
source: or alpha-synuclein or TDP-43 in AD (Arai et al., 2009; Hamilton, 2006; Spires-Jones et al., 2017; Attems and Jellinger, 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Associations between vascular factors and neurodegenerative dementias such as AD are common.
source: Also, associations between vascular factors and neurodegenerative dementias such as AD are common (Kalaria, 2009; Sweeney et al., 2018),
evidence: Supported by citations to Kalaria, 2009 and Sweeney et al., 2018.

claim: In MS, retrograde neurodegeneration secondary to focal damage from remote lesions, iron accumulation in the deep gray matter and 'virtual hypoxia' in the hub regions could all potentially combine and contribute to explain observed neurodegeneration.
source: Further, in MS, retrograde neurodegeneration secondary to focal damage from remote lesions, iron accumulation in the deep gray matter and 'virtual hypoxia' in the hub regions could all potentially combine and contribute to explain observed neurodegeneration (Trapp and Stys, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trapp and Stys, 2009.

claim: Considering only end-stage pathology severely limits sensitivity.
source: Regarding limitation (ii), considering only end-stage pathology severely limits sensitivity — like trying to guess the plot of a movie after watching only the final scene (Oxtoby and Alexander, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Oxtoby and Alexander, 2017.

claim: The GP Progression Model estimates trajectories of atrophy evolution that reflect observed atrophy patterns in each cohort (AD, PPMS and HA).
source: In this section, we show first that the GP Progression Model estimates trajectories of atrophy evolution that reflect observed atrophy patterns in each cohort (AD, PPMS and HA).
evidence: Demonstrated by Figure 2 and supporting text describing the progression patterns.

claim: The topological profiles derived from atrophy evolution patterns are distinct for each condition.
source: Secondly, we show that the topological profiles derived from such atrophy evolution patterns are distinct for each condition and explain observations better than profiles estimated when using end-stage data only, and better than single topological descriptors.
evidence: Demonstrated by Table 1 showing different weights for each condition and AIC scores in Figure 2.

claim: Topological profiles explain observations better than profiles estimated when using end-stage data only.
source: Secondly, we show that the topological profiles derived from such atrophy evolution patterns are distinct for each condition and explain observations better than profiles estimated when using end-stage data only, and better than single topological descriptors.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of Figure 3(a-b) with Figure 3(e-f) and Table 3 showing higher classification rates.

claim: Topological profiles explain observations better than single topological descriptors.
source: Secondly, we show that the topological profiles derived from such atrophy evolution patterns are distinct for each condition and explain observations better than profiles estimated when using end-stage data only, and better than single topological descriptors.
evidence: Demonstrated by AIC scores in Figure 2 and variance explained percentages in the text.

claim: Most individual profiles reflect their corresponding cohort profile.
source: Further, we demonstrate that most individual profiles reflect their corresponding cohort profile (and neurological condition), and that those that do not ('outliers') show clinical characteristics of the topologically-nearest cohort.
evidence: Demonstrated by Figure 3 and Table 3 showing high classification rates.

claim: Individual profiles that do not match their cohort profile ('outliers') show clinical characteristics of the topologically-nearest cohort.
source: Further, we demonstrate that most individual profiles reflect their corresponding cohort profile (and neurological condition), and that those that do not ('outliers') show clinical characteristics of the topologically-nearest cohort.
evidence: Demonstrated by ANOVA analyses showing AD outliers closer to HA have higher MMSE scores and HA outliers closer to AD have lower MMSE scores and higher dementia incidence.

claim: In the AD cohort, the first regions to show atrophy are the superior temporal region and the hippocampus.
source: In the AD cohort, the first regions to show atrophy are the superior temporal region and the hippocampus, followed by the amygdala, the remaining temporal regions, the insular and the supramarginal regions, and then the precentral and postcentral regions and the posterior lobe.
evidence: Demonstrated by Figure 2 top row left panel showing the temporal progression of atrophy in AD.

claim: The estimated AD progression gradually involves the occipital lobe, the middle frontal region, and finally the remaining subcortical areas, with thalamus and caudate last.
source: The estimated progression gradually involves the occipital lobe, the middle frontal region, and finally the remaining subcortical areas, with thalamus and caudate last, which matches well-known atrophy progression patterns observed in AD from post-mortem histology (Eshaghi et al., 2018b) and in-vivo disease progression models (Donohue et al., 2014; Fonteijn et al., 2012; Hinrichs et al., 2011; Desikan et al., 2006).
evidence: Demonstrated by Figure 2 and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The AD atrophy progression pattern matches well-known atrophy progression patterns observed in AD from post-mortem histology and in-vivo disease progression models.
source: The estimated progression gradually involves the occipital lobe, the middle frontal region, and finally the remaining subcortical areas, with thalamus and caudate last, which matches well-known atrophy progression patterns observed in AD from post-mortem histology (Eshaghi et al., 2018b) and in-vivo disease progression models (Donohue et al., 2014; Fonteijn et al., 2012; Hinrichs et al., 2011; Desikan et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In PPMS, the progression first involves some subcortical areas (caudate, thalamus, pallidum).
source: In PPMS, the progression first involves some subcortical areas (caudate, thalamus, pallidum), followed by the superior parietal region, the remaining subcortical areas (amygdala, putamen, nucleus accumbens), few frontal regions (mostly middle- and orbito-frontal), the precentral, and then the occipital and temporal lobes, which become abnormal later in the progression.
evidence: Demonstrated by Figure 2 top row middle panel showing the temporal progression of atrophy in PPMS.

claim: The PPMS progression dynamics agree with recent results obtained using a different DPM.
source: The dynamics of progression agree with recent results (Eshaghi et al., 2018a; Vinke et al., 2018), obtained using a different DPM.
evidence: Supported by citations to Eshaghi et al., 2018a and Vinke et al., 2018.

claim: In the HA cohort, early involvement is observed in the insula, the superior and middle temporal lobes, the middle frontal, and the putamen.
source: In the HA cohort, we observe early involvement of the insula, the superior and middle temporal lobes, the middle frontal, and the putamen.
evidence: Demonstrated by Figure 2 top row right panel showing the temporal progression in HA.

claim: The HA progression pattern agrees with other studies of volume loss in normal aging.
source: This agrees with other studies of volume loss in normal aging (Narvacan et al., 2017; Watson et al., 2016; Akaike, 1974).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: AD shows a topological profile with concurrency of centrality metrics (40%) and network proximity (60%).
source: Specifically, AD shows a concurrency of centrality metrics (40%) and network proximity (60%);
evidence: Derived from Table 1 showing the weights of topological descriptors for AD.

claim: PPMS shows a topological profile with presence of centrality (35%), segregation (45%) and cortical proximity (20%).
source: PPMS shows a more complex profile with presence of centrality (35%), segregation (45%) and cortical proximity (20%);
evidence: Derived from Table 1 showing the weights of topological descriptors for PPMS.

claim: HA shows a topological profile matching a combination of centrality (25%), cortical proximity (60%) and constant progression (20%).
source: HA matches a combination of centrality (25%), cortical proximity (60%) and constant progression (20%).
evidence: Derived from Table 1 showing the weights of topological descriptors for HA.

claim: The topological profiles for AD, PPMS and HA differ substantially.
source: Table 1 shows that the topological profiles for AD, PPMS and HA differ substantially.
evidence: Demonstrated by the different weight distributions in Table 1.

claim: In the AD cohort, the topological profile explains 82% of the variance.
source: Indeed, in the AD cohort, the topological profile explains 82% of the variance, with the constant term explaining just 6%, in contrast to 51% explained by network proximity.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of model fit presented in the Results section.

claim: In the AD cohort, network proximity explains 51% of the variance.
source: Indeed, in the AD cohort, the topological profile explains 82% of the variance, with the constant term explaining just 6%, in contrast to 51% explained by network proximity.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of model fit presented in the Results section.

claim: In the PPMS cohort, the topological profile explains 83% of the variance.
source: In the PPMS cohort, the topological profile explains 83%, the constant term 7%, and inverse clustering 25%.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of model fit presented in the Results section.

claim: In the PPMS cohort, inverse clustering explains 25% of the variance.
source: In the PPMS cohort, the topological profile explains 83%, the constant term 7%, and inverse clustering 25%.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of model fit presented in the Results section.

claim: In the HA cohort, the topological profile explains 88% of the variance.
source: Similarly, in the HA cohort the topological profile explains 88%, the constant term 16%, and cortical proximity 64%.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of model fit presented in the Results section.

claim: In the HA cohort, cortical proximity explains 64% of the variance.
source: Similarly, in the HA cohort the topological profile explains 88%, the constant term 16%, and cortical proximity 64%.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of model fit presented in the Results section.

claim: The three cohorts separate well in topological space.
source: Figure 3(a) and (b) show that (i) the cohort topological profiles are consistent under bootstrap cross-validation, (ii) the three cohorts separate well in topological space, and iii) individual profiles group around cohort profiles.
evidence: Demonstrated by Figure 3(a) and (b) showing distinct clustering of cohorts.

claim: The cohort topological profiles are consistent under bootstrap cross-validation.
source: Figure 3(a) and (b) show that (i) the cohort topological profiles are consistent under bootstrap cross-validation, (ii) the three cohorts separate well in topological space, and iii) individual profiles group around cohort profiles.
evidence: Demonstrated by small stars in Figure 3(b) showing tight clustering of bootstrapped cohort profiles.

claim: Individual profiles group around cohort profiles.
source: Figure 3(a) and (b) show that (i) the cohort topological profiles are consistent under bootstrap cross-validation, (ii) the three cohorts separate well in topological space, and iii) individual profiles group around cohort profiles.
evidence: Demonstrated by Figure 3(a) and (b) showing clustering of individual profiles around cohort profiles.

claim: When using only late-stage atrophy to identify topological profiles, the cohorts separate less strongly than using the DPM topological profiles.
source: Figure 3(e) and (f) show that when using only late-stage atrophy to identify topological profiles: i) the cohorts separate less strongly than using the DPM topological profiles (see Supplementary file 1- Table S2);
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of Figure 3(e-f) with Figure 3(a-b) and Supplementary file 1- Table S2.

claim: When using only late-stage atrophy, the rate of assignment of AD and PPMS individual profiles to the corresponding cohort profile is lower than using GP Progression Model-driven topological profiles.
source: and ii) the rate of assignment of AD and PPMS individual profiles to the corresponding cohort profile is lower than using GP Progression Model-driven topological profiles and with a greater fraction of outliers (see Table 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by Table 3 showing lower classification rates for late-stage profiles (in parentheses).

claim: Late-stage information alone is not sufficient to provide distinct topological profiles.
source: Both observations suggest that late-stage information alone is not sufficient to provide distinct topological profiles.
evidence: Inference based on the comparison of full-course vs. late-stage results shown in Figure 3 and Table 3.

claim: 159 AD-cohort individuals (130 MCI, 29 probable AD) are closer to the HA cohort-level profile out of 1312 MCI+AD patients.
source: Figure 3(a) identifies 159 AD-cohort outliers (130 MCI, 29 probable AD) closer to the HA cohort-level profile, out of 1312 MCI+AD patients.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of outliers identified from Figure 3(a).

claim: AD outliers closer to the HA profile exhibit a higher MMSE score (27.6 ± 1.2 vs 26.1 ± 1.7) than the rest of the AD cohort.
source: An ANOVA 1-way test between the two groups was performed and differences were found in MMSE, where the outliers exhibit a higher MMSE score (27.6 ± 1.2 vs 26.1 ± 1.7).
evidence: Statistical analysis (ANOVA) of clinical features comparing outliers to non-outliers.

claim: AD outliers closer to the HA profile score lower on the Clinical Dementia Rating Scale (1.8 ± 0.7 vs 2.1 ± 0.3) than the rest of the AD cohort.
source: Slight differences were found in the Clinical Dementia Rating Scale, with outliers scoring lower (1.8 ± 0.7 vs 2.1 ± 0.3).
evidence: Statistical analysis (ANOVA) of clinical features comparing outliers to non-outliers.

claim: AD outliers closer to the HA profile have reduced cognitive deficits compared to inliers, on average.
source: Both results show that the outliers have reduced cognitive deficits compared to inliers, on average.
evidence: Inference based on MMSE and Clinical Dementia Rating Scale results.

claim: 358 of 5463 HA individuals are closer to the AD cohort profile.
source: Figure 3(a) identifies 358 of 5463 HA individuals closer to the AD cohort profile.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of outliers identified from Figure 3(a).

claim: HA outliers closer to the AD profile exhibit a lower MMSE score (27.7 ± 0.8 vs 28.0 ± 0.6) than the rest of the HA group.
source: An ANOVA 1-way test between these outliers and the rest of the HA group found differences in MMSE, where the outliers exhibit a lower MMSE score (27.7 ± 0.8 vs 28.0 ± 0.6);
evidence: Statistical analysis (ANOVA) of clinical features comparing outliers to non-outliers.

claim: HA outliers closer to the AD profile are older (70.5 ± 10.1 vs 64.5 ± 9.8) than the rest of the HA group.
source: and a difference in age, with the outliers being older (70.5 ± 10.1 vs 64.5 ± 9.8).
evidence: Statistical analysis (ANOVA) of demographic features comparing outliers to non-outliers.

claim: Of 148 HA individuals who developed dementia after 2-4 years, 105 reside in the HA-AD outlier group, which thus contains 70% of the individuals with prodromal dementia.
source: Of those 148 individuals, 105 reside in the HA-AD outlier group, which thus contains 70% of the individuals with prodromal dementia; in contrast the non-outlier group consists of only 5% prodromal dementia cases.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of prodromal dementia incidence in outliers vs. non-outliers.

claim: The non-outlier HA group consists of only 5% prodromal dementia cases.
source: Of those 148 individuals, 105 reside in the HA-AD outlier group, which thus contains 70% of the individuals with prodromal dementia; in contrast the non-outlier group consists of only 5% prodromal dementia cases.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of prodromal dementia incidence in outliers vs. non-outliers.

claim: No significant differences were found between PPMS outliers and the rest of the PPMS group.
source: We also analyzed PPMS with respect to both AD and HA: the analysis returned 53 AD individuals closer to PPMS; 1 PPMS individual closer to AD; 13 PPMS individuals closer to HA and 100 HA individuals closer to PPMS. No significant differences were found between any subgroups, for any comparisons:
evidence: Statistical analysis (ANOVA) found no significant differences in clinical or demographic features.

claim: The distance of individual profiles from the cohort profile correlates negatively with MMSE for the AD cohort (R = 0.11, p<0.01).
source: Finally and more generally, we analyzed features extracted from topological profiles, in particular, the distance of individual profiles from the cohort profile, and show that they correlate negatively with individual cohort-specific clinical features. Specifically, MMSE for the AD cohort (R = 0.11, p<0.01);
evidence: Correlation analysis between topological profile features and clinical measures.

claim: The distance of individual profiles from the cohort profile correlates negatively with EDSS for PPMS (R = 0.68, p=0.07).
source: Specifically, MMSE for the AD cohort (R = 0.11, p<0.01); EDSS for PPMS (R = 0.68, p=0.07);
evidence: Correlation analysis between topological profile features and clinical measures.

claim: The distance of individual profiles from the cohort profile correlates negatively with age for HA (R = 0.32, p<0.01).
source: and age for HA (R = 0.32, p<0.01).
evidence: Correlation analysis between topological profile features and demographic measures.

claim: Combinations of topological descriptors explain observations better than any individual descriptor.
source: We showed that combinations of topological descriptors explain observations better than any individual descriptor and that the combinations representative of each condition, despite some commonality as suggested in Soto and Pritzkow (2018), Jucker and Walker (2018) and Fu et al. (2018), differ substantially both at the cohort and individual level.
evidence: Summary of results demonstrated throughout the manuscript with AIC scores and variance explained.

claim: The combinations of topological descriptors representative of each condition differ substantially both at the cohort and individual level.
source: We showed that combinations of topological descriptors explain observations better than any individual descriptor and that the combinations representative of each condition, despite some commonality as suggested in Soto and Pritzkow (2018), Jucker and Walker (2018) and Fu et al. (2018), differ substantially both at the cohort and individual level.
evidence: Demonstrated by Table 1 showing different weight distributions and Figure 3 showing separation in topological space.

claim: The differences in topological profiles go beyond simple observations that the pattern of atrophy accumulation is different in these three cohorts.
source: We emphasize that these differences go beyond simple observations that the pattern of atrophy accumulation is different in these three cohorts, which could arise simply from equivalent spreading mechanisms from different epicentres; our results go further by strongly suggesting distinct modes of dependence of the pathological spread on the underlying connectivity.
evidence: Inference based on the analysis of topological profiles showing different combinations of descriptors.

claim: Using the full disease time-course estimated via a GP Progression Model produces better-defined topological profiles than using only late-stage atrophy.
source: We also show that using the full disease time-course, estimated via a GP Progression Model (Desikan et al., 2006) produces better-defined topological profiles than using only late-stage atrophy.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of results in Figure 3 and Table 3 for full-course vs. late-stage profiles.

claim: There is significant correlation between features of the topological profiles and individual clinical or demographic features.
source: Further, we retrieved significant correlation between features of the topological profiles and individual clinical or demographic features, suggesting potential clinical utility of the topological profile.
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation analyses showing relationships with MMSE, EDSS, and age.

claim: The outliers in the AD-HA comparison display characteristics that align them with the other cohort.
source: Finally, we showed that the outliers in the AD-HA comparison display characteristics that align them with the other cohort, providing evidence that our topological profiles reflect underlying disease processes, and indicating potential use of the topological profile to highlight disease risk.
evidence: Demonstrated by ANOVA analyses showing AD outliers have HA-like cognitive scores and HA outliers have AD-like cognitive scores and dementia incidence.

claim: Graph-theoretic measures may associate with different mechanisms of disease spread in neural networks.
source: As discussed in the introduction, one key implication here (as in previous literature Raj et al., 2012; Raj et al., 2015; Seeley et al., 2009; de Haan et al., 2012) is that graph-theoretic measures may associate with different mechanisms of disease spread in neural networks.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and the conceptual framework of the study.

claim: The AD topological profile supports recent results that identify neuronal distance from epicentre (or trans-neuronal spread) as the principal topological descriptor of neurodegeneration in AD.
source: The AD topological profile identified here supports recent results that identify neuronal distance from epicentre (or trans-neuronal spread) as the principal topological descriptor of neurodegeneration in AD (Jucker and Walker, 2018; Jucker and Walker, 2013; Cope et al., 2018; Raj et al., 2015; Weickenmeier et al., 2019).
evidence: The AD profile shows 60% network proximity component, consistent with prior literature.

claim: Both cohort- and individual-level AD profiles show a substantial additional component of neurodegeneration due to centrality metrics — vulnerability of brain network hubs.
source: However, both cohort- and individual-level profiles also show a substantial additional component of neurodegeneration due to centrality metrics — vulnerability of brain network hubs.
evidence: The AD profile shows 40% centrality component as shown in Table 1.

claim: The centrality component in AD has not clearly been highlighted previously because it is less apparent in a topological profile estimated from only late-stage atrophy data.
source: This component has not clearly been highlighted previously, because a) it is less apparent in a topological profile estimated from only late-stage atrophy data, and b) it is suppressed when using the previous single-descriptor approach.
evidence: Demonstrated by Table 2 showing reduced centrality component (25% vs 40%) in late-stage profiles.

claim: The centrality component in AD is suppressed when using the previous single-descriptor approach.
source: This component has not clearly been highlighted previously, because a) it is less apparent in a topological profile estimated from only late-stage atrophy data, and b) it is suppressed when using the previous single-descriptor approach.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of topological profile results with single-descriptor results.

claim: Hub-vulnerability may drive early phases of AD progression while neuronal distance from the epicentre dominates later stages.
source: This might arise from metabolic demand increasing primarily during early degeneration so that hub-vulnerability drives early phases of the progression pattern (Alladi et al., 2007), while neuronal distance from the epicentre dominates later stages.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed differences between full-course and late-stage profiles, supported by citation.

claim: The early centrality component of the AD topological profile suggests that pathology may start around local hubs.
source: This finding might also explain some aspects of the biological heterogeneity of AD, which produces high variance in atrophy patterns across individuals. In particular, the early centrality component of the topological profile suggests that pathology may start around local hubs, which is consistent with the focal presentation of atrophy in atypical Alzheimer's diseases such as posterior cortical atrophy or progressive aphasia (Du, 2006; Mendez et al., 2002; Barnham et al., 2004).
evidence: Speculation based on the centrality component in the profile, supported by citations to atypical AD presentations.

claim: The early centrality component is consistent with the focal presentation of atrophy in atypical Alzheimer's diseases such as posterior cortical atrophy or progressive aphasia.
source: In particular, the early centrality component of the topological profile suggests that pathology may start around local hubs, which is consistent with the focal presentation of atrophy in atypical Alzheimer's diseases such as posterior cortical atrophy or progressive aphasia (Du, 2006; Mendez et al., 2002; Barnham et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies of atypical AD.

claim: In HA and PPMS, hub vulnerability appears as a significant component only when considering the full trajectory rather than only late-stage atrophy.
source: Similarly, in HA and PPMS, hub vulnerability appears as a significant component only when considering the full trajectory rather than only late-stage atrophy.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of Table 1 (full-course) with Table 2 (late-stage) showing reduced centrality components in late-stage profiles.

claim: Activity-dependent mechanisms such as oxidative stress, microglial activation, neurovascular dysfunction or 'virtual hypoxia' may influence early brain loss across a range of neurodegenerative conditions.
source: This may suggest that activity-dependent mechanisms, such as oxidative stress (Cagnin et al., 2001), microglial activation (Hickman et al., 2018; Chiaravalloti and DeLuca, 2008), neurovascular dysfunction (Sweeney et al., 2018) or 'virtual hypoxia' (Trapp and Stys, 2009) influence early brain loss across a range of neurodegenerative conditions.
evidence: Speculation based on the centrality component observed across conditions, supported by citations.

claim: Departures of individual profiles from that of the corresponding cohort may signal abnormality with respect to their cohort.
source: Our results indicate that departures of individual profiles from that of the corresponding cohort may signal abnormality with respect to their cohort, while alignment with another cohort-level profile may correspond to clinical features of that other cohort.
evidence: Inference based on the outlier analyses showing clinical differences.

claim: Alignment of individual profiles with another cohort-level profile may correspond to clinical features of that other cohort.
source: Our results indicate that departures of individual profiles from that of the corresponding cohort may signal abnormality with respect to their cohort, while alignment with another cohort-level profile may correspond to clinical features of that other cohort.
evidence: Demonstrated by ANOVA analyses showing outliers have clinical features of the other cohort.

claim: Neurodegeneration in AD and PPMS is not simply an acceleration of the aging process.
source: Overall, our results suggest that neurodegeneration in AD and PPMS is not simply an acceleration of the aging process, but that the two diseases have distinct topological profiles of neurodegeneration, which differ from those of HA.
evidence: Inference based on the distinct topological profiles shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: AD and PPMS have distinct topological profiles of neurodegeneration, which differ from those of HA.
source: Overall, our results suggest that neurodegeneration in AD and PPMS is not simply an acceleration of the aging process, but that the two diseases have distinct topological profiles of neurodegeneration, which differ from those of HA.
evidence: Demonstrated by Table 1 showing different weight distributions and Figure 3 showing separation in topological space.

claim: The cohort and individual-level topological profiles identified for AD and PPMS are clearly distinct from one another.
source: The cohort and individual-level topological profiles we identify for AD and PPMS are clearly distinct from one another.
evidence: Demonstrated by Table 1 and Figure 3 showing different profiles and separation in topological space.

claim: The PPMS profile has diverse contributing mechanisms including centrality, segregation and cortical proximity, suggesting that many different processes are at play.
source: The AD topological profile is a combination of centrality and network proximity, while the PPMS profile has diverse contributing mechanisms including centrality, segregation and cortical proximity, suggesting that many different processes are at play.
evidence: Demonstrated by Table 1 showing PPMS has contributions from centrality (35%), segregation (45%), and cortical proximity (20%).

claim: The HA topological profile has a strong component of both the cortical proximity and the constant propagation mechanisms, suggesting relatively uniform loss across the brain that is not linked to any particular brain-connectivity feature.
source: Also, both separate from the HA topological profile, which has a strong component of both the cortical proximity and the constant propagation mechanisms, suggesting relatively uniform loss across the brain that is not linked to any particular brain-connectivity feature.
evidence: Demonstrated by Table 1 showing HA has cortical proximity (60%) and constant progression (20%) components.

claim: The effects of ageing were regressed out in the AD and PPMS cohort in order to minimize the effects of the ageing process on disease models.
source: Further, we note that we have regressed out the effects of ageing in the AD and PPMS cohort in order to minimize the effects of the ageing process on disease models.
evidence: Description of preprocessing steps in the Methods section.

claim: Mechanisms, in addition to actual atrophy patterns, are distinct in AD and PPMS from those underpinning normal aging.
source: These observations underline the idea that mechanisms, in addition to actual atrophy patterns, are distinct in these diseases from those underpinning normal aging.
evidence: Inference based on the distinct topological profiles observed for AD, PPMS, and HA.

claim: Structural connectome estimation using tractography is prone to false positive and negative connections that can influence subsequent predictions.
source: For example, structural connectome estimation using tractography is prone to false positive and negative connections (Thomas et al., 2014; Petersen et al., 2017) that can influence subsequent predictions.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on tractography limitations.

claim: Tractography reliably recovers at least many of the major known anatomical connections sufficiently well to highlight broad differences in atrophy patterns associated to the different mechanisms.
source: Nevertheless, tractography does reliably recover at least many of the major known anatomical connections sufficiently well to highlight broad differences in atrophy patterns associated to the different mechanisms.
evidence: Inference based on the successful application of tractography-derived connectomes in this study.

claim: The choice of connectome (young and healthy or subject-specific) does not significantly impact the predictive ability of a model for trans-synaptic transmission of toxic proteins in AD.
source: This decision is also supported by recent results in AD showing that the choice of connectome (young and healthy or subject-specific) does not significantly impact the predictive ability of a model for trans-synaptic transmission of toxic proteins (Acosta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Acosta et al., 2018.

claim: Using the healthy connectome as the substrate for propagation is a sensible first-order approximation.
source: We believe using the healthy connectome as the substrate for propagation is a sensible first-order approximation.
evidence: Inference based on the discussion of connectome choice and supporting evidence.

claim: The GP Progression Model captures the trajectory of change in biomarker values rather than underlying pathology.
source: One additional caveat of using the GP Progression Model is that the model captures the trajectory of change in biomarker values rather than underlying pathology;
evidence: Discussion of model limitations based on understanding of the GP Progression Model.

claim: Differences among biomarker accuracy can make the order of biomarker change depart from the order of underlying pathological change.
source: differences among biomarker accuracy (e.g. higher noise in volume measurements of smaller regions) can make the order of biomarker change depart from the order of underlying pathological change, although we expect such effects tend to be small with our processing pipeline – see Fonteijn et al. (2012) and Hinrichs et al. (2011) for further discussion.
evidence: Discussion of potential limitations supported by citations.

claim: The epicentre for disease propagation may vary among patients in a particular disease class.
source: In addition to variation in the structural connectome discussed above, the epicentre for disease propagation may vary among patients in a particular disease class and a number of recent works explore methods for per-subject epicentre selection (Young et al., 2014; Young et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on epicentre selection.

claim: A single cohort-level epicentre was estimated as the most atrophied region for each data set.
source: Here, we estimated a single cohort-level epicentre as the most atrophied region for each data set, and each reflected common knowledge of brain tissue loss in AD, PPMS and HA.
evidence: Description of the method used in this study.

claim: The epicentres identified (hippocampus for AD, caudate for PPMS, insula for HA) reflected common knowledge of brain tissue loss in AD, PPMS and HA.
source: Here, we estimated a single cohort-level epicentre as the most atrophied region for each data set, and each reflected common knowledge of brain tissue loss in AD, PPMS and HA.
evidence: The epicentres are consistent with prior knowledge as stated in the text.

claim: Individually selected epicentres in a number of neurodegenerative diseases are always seated in or near the most atrophied region.
source: Our epicentres broadly agree with (Zhou et al., 2012), who found that individually selected epicentres in a number of neurodegenerative diseases are always seated in or near the most atrophied region.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2012.

claim: Topological profiles may provide useful information in the clinic with further development and experiments.
source: With further development and experiments, topological profiles may also provide useful information in the clinic.
evidence: Speculation about future clinical applications based on current results.

claim: AD-like HA outliers may be considered at risk for AD.
source: For example, AD-like HA outliers may be considered at risk for AD and decisions could be informed by this, including patient management (more frequent visits to monitor the patient) and recruitment into clinical studies/trials.
evidence: Speculation about potential clinical applications based on the finding that HA outliers closer to AD have higher dementia incidence.

claim: The ADNI study collected longitudinal measurements for all available ADNI 1/GO/2 individuals with at least one 'quality control' flagged 3D-T1 MRI scan.
source: We collected longitudinal measurements for all the available ADNI 1/GO/2 individuals with at least one 'quality control' flagged 3D-T1 MRI scan.
evidence: Description of data collection procedures.

claim: The AD cohort includes 1713 subjects with 'HC', 'MCI' or 'AD' diagnosis.
source: Subject with no available diagnosis were discarded, thus leaving us 1713 subjects, with 'HC', 'MCI' or 'AD' diagnosis.
evidence: Description of the study cohort.

claim: The mean age of the AD cohort is 73.9 (7.2) years.
source: The subjects included in our analysis are 1713; the mean (std) age of the cohort is 73.9 (7.2) years.
evidence: Demographic description of the study cohort.

claim: The PPMS study includes 44 individuals with primary progressive multiple sclerosis and 20 healthy controls.
source: The participants include 44 individuals with primary progressive multiple sclerosis (PPMS) and 20 healthy controls (HC).
evidence: Description of the study cohort.

claim: The mean age of the PPMS cohort is 41.6 (10.2) years.
source: The longitudinal data set used for this study consisted in 64 individuals; the mean (std) age of the cohort is 41.6 (10.2) years.
evidence: Demographic description of the study cohort.

claim: The Rotterdam Study is a prospective cohort study ongoing since 1990 in the city of Rotterdam in The Netherlands.
source: The Rotterdam Study is a prospective cohort study ongoing since 1990 in the city of Rotterdam in The Netherlands.
evidence: Description of the Rotterdam Study.

claim: The HA cohort contains 148 individuals that would develop dementia in the 2–4 years follow-up(s).
source: The study contains 148 individuals that would develop dementia in the 2–4 years follow-up(s).
evidence: Description of the study cohort.

claim: The HA cohort consists of 5463 individuals with a mean age of 64.8 (10.8) years.
source: The longitudinal data set used for this study consisted in 5463 individuals; the mean (std) age of the cohort is 64.8 (10.8) years.
evidence: Demographic description of the study cohort.

claim: Structural connectomes were generated using tools provided in the MRtrix3 software package.
source: Structural connectomes were generated using tools provided in the MRtrix3 software package (http://mrtrix.org).
evidence: Description of methods used for connectome generation.

claim: The anatomical connectome is a weighted adjacency matrix that includes only inter-node connections across the 82 ROIs consisting of cortical and subcortical gray-matter regions, excluding the cerebellum and brain stem.
source: Our anatomical connectome for each participant is a weighted adjacency matrix that includes only inter-node connections across the 82 ROIs consisting of cortical and subcortical gray-matter regions, excluding the cerebellum and brain stem.
evidence: Description of the connectome construction.

claim: The average structural adjacency matrix was computed by taking the mean over the subject-wise matrices.
source: The average structural adjacency matrix was computed by taking the mean over the subject-wise matrices.
evidence: Description of the method for creating the average connectome.

claim: The problem of estimating β is solved via Expectation-Maximization, which becomes an iterative-multiplicative algorithm also known as ISRA.
source: We solve the problem via Expectation-Maximization, which, in the positively-constrained least-squared case, has a simple closed form, and becomes an iterative-multiplicative algorithm also known as ISRA (Daube-Witherspoon and Muehllehner, 1986; Dempster et al., 1977).
evidence: Description of the optimization method with citations.
